A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Sharp Matrix Empirical Bernstein Inequalities by the same authors. All 17 pages of v1 and 20 pages of v3, including equations, tables and appendices, support comparison without material reading gaps.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical inequalities, proofs and analytical comparisons, including Appendices A and B, but no original experimental or simulation outcomes. Its numerical percentage in Appendix B is an analytical calculation.

after.justification: v3 reports original matrix simulations in Section 5.3 and Table 1, and scalar simulations in Appendix B and Table 2.

M1.justification: The two main constructions remain. However, Eq. (37) changes the initial variance proxy from V0 = 0 to V0 = I/4, affecting the first weight. Eq. (18) also replaces log(2d/alpha) with log(2nd/alpha) in the variance-correction terms, changing the computed confidence radius.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical evaluation coverage. v3 introduces synthetic mean-estimation evaluations for i.i.d. 3-by-3 matrices with fixed orthonormal projections and independent uniform eigenvalues, plus uniform scalar observations. These are actual new evaluations; the broader martingale assumptions are not tested experimentally.

E2.justification: Previously analytical comparisons gain numerical evaluations. Table 1 compares both proposed matrix bounds against Tropp's oracle Bennett-Bernstein bound. Table 2 compares the proposed Sharp MP bound with Original MP and the Waudby-Smith–Ramdas self-normalized bound, using the scalar oracle as reference. These comparator combinations were not numerically evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: v3 introduces a numerical evaluation design using confidence-set length divided by oracle length, alpha = 0.05, and sample sizes 100, 1,000, 10,000, 100,000 and 1,000,000. These settings belong to new simulations, rather than revisions or reruns of existing experiments.

E4.justification: The new sample-size sweeps examine how quickly the bounds approach the oracle and when asymptotic sharpening becomes advantageous. This adds a limited convergence and sensitivity analysis within the two uniform-data setups.

E5.justification: Neither version reports simulation run counts, seeds, variability across repetitions or statistical tests. The 95% confidence levels in v3 define the confidence sets being compared; they do not quantify uncertainty in the tabulated simulation results.

E6.justification: Both numerical tables are new. At n = 1,000, Table 1 reports oracle-relative lengths of 2.315 and 1.120 for the first and second matrix bounds. Table 2 shows Sharp MP initially worse than Original MP, but at n = 1,000,000 their ratios are 1.021 and 1.121, versus 1.002 for self-normalization. v1 has no corresponding simulation results.

T1.justification: Corollary 4.3 replaces i.i.d. assumptions with constant conditional mean and variance under adaptation. New Lemma A.2 and Appendix A.3 supply matrix inequalities, a martingale strong law and consistency results; Appendix A.4 substantially expands the asymptotic derivation. Eq. (18) corrects the logarithms required by the union-bound split. The new minimizer formula in Eq. (45), however, has mismatched summation limits.

C1.justification: Although the abstract and two principal constructions remain, Proposition 1.2 broadens the central sharp-adaptation claim from i.i.d. observations to common conditional variance under martingale dependence. Section 6 additionally claims a practical advantage for the second matrix bound, citing lengths only 12% and 2.6% above the oracle at n = 1,000 and 10,000.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the simulations as showing faster convergence to oracle length for self-normalization and a large-sample benefit from sharpening the scalar MP bound. Section 4 gives a more explicit weighted least-squares rationale for prediction. Existing limitations concerning lower-order terms and effective-rank bounds remain.

D1.justification: Section 5.3 newly documents the matrix simulation's dimension, fixed projections and independent uniform eigenvalues; Appendix B identifies the scalar generating distribution. Section 4 explicitly writes out the previously recommended weighted predictor. No code, software, hardware or runtime information is added.

R1.justification: New Appendix C substantially expands positioning against scalar PAC-Bayes and betting bounds, discussing Tolstikhin–Seldin, Mhammedi and coauthors, Jang and coauthors, Alquier, and Shekhar–Ramdas. Hall–Heyde is added for martingale limit theory. Section 5.1 also positions the revised asymptotics as relaxing the i.i.d. assumption of Waudby-Smith–Ramdas.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order remain. v3 expands the weight-selection explanation and summary, renames Section 5 to Comparisons, and inserts a simulation subsection, a consistency subsection and Appendix C. These are localized structural and explanatory changes rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 adds two compact numerical tables with captions, additional displayed equations and boxed terms in the expanded proof. Existing material reflows around these additions, while the overall single-column design remains. Neither version contains figures.

improvement.justification: Correcting Eq. (18) aligns the finite-sample radius with its stated union-bound allocation. The added consistency arguments, literature discussion and simulations make the theoretical scope and finite-sample tradeoffs easier to assess. These gains are limited by narrow simulation coverage without repetition or uncertainty reporting, and a new indexing error in Eq. (45), whose numerator sums to n while its denominator sums to n-1. The net improvement is supported but limited.
